passage:
"Neelam, it's almost midnight. Still on the essay?"
"Papa, it's due at eight. I've written one paragraph."
"Show me."
"It's bad. Manoj said he'll send me his from last year. Same topic."
Manoj Uncle's son had topped the class. Papa sat down. "And then?"
"And then I change some words."
"Would your teacher know?"
"Maybe not." She paused. "Maybe yes. She reads everything twice."
"And would you know?"
Neelam rolled her eyes. "Papa, don't do the philosophy thing."
"Fine. What's your one paragraph about?"
"How rivers shaped old towns." She looked at it again. "Actually, I had one more idea about the ghats."
"Write that. I'll make tea."
She groaned, but she deleted Manoj's message without opening it.

qa.q: What was Neelam's essay about?
qa.a: It was about how rivers shaped old towns.

qa.q: Why did Neelam roll her eyes at "And would you know?"
qa.a: She was tired and a bit defensive, but the question also pricked her, because she knew copying would feel dishonest to her.

qa.q: What worked about Papa's way of handling the temptation?
qa.a: He asked questions instead of lecturing, then turned her attention back to her own ideas and offered tea, so she chose not to copy.

qa.q: What would change if Neelam had used Manoj's essay?
qa.a: She might have finished faster but risked being caught, and she would have missed writing her own idea about the ghats.

grounding: It shows a teen tempted to copy an old essay late at night choosing to write her own with a parent's gentle questions.

passage: Last term I almost handed in an essay I didn't write. I'm Parveen. The topic was on the causes of the First World War, and I had three other tests that week. My classmate Nikita showed me how an AI tool could produce a full essay in a minute. It looked perfect. I pasted mine in, read it, and felt nothing. It didn't sound like me at all. It had words I'd never use. Then I thought about Ma'am's comment on my last essay: "I like how you argue." This one didn't argue anything. So I closed it and wrote my own at 1 am. It was messier. Ma'am gave it a B and wrote, "Your voice is back." Nikita got caught. I felt sorry for her, honestly.

qa.q: What grade did Parveen's essay get?
qa.a: It got a B.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel nothing reading the AI-written essay?
qa.a: It didn't sound like her or carry her own arguments, so it felt empty and not really hers.

qa.q: What helped Parveen resist the shortcut?
qa.a: Remembering her teacher's praise for how she argues reminded her that her own voice was worth more than a perfect-looking copy.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel after getting caught?
qa.a: She is probably embarrassed and worried, and may wish she had written her own even if it was messier.

grounding: A teen reflects on resisting an AI-written essay and valuing her own original voice.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9:
During the science project week, I noticed that Zubin's report looked very similar to Ishita's from the other section. Same diagrams, same unusual phrases. I spoke to both separately. Ishita was upset; she had lent her notebook to Zubin to "get an idea." Zubin admitted he had copied large parts. He looked at the floor and said, "I didn't think it was a big deal."
I explained that it wasn't fair to Ishita, and that the project was meant to help him learn, not just produce a report. I gave him three extra days to redo it himself and asked him to apologise to Ishita.
Follow-up: His new report was shorter but his own. Ishita said they're still friends.

qa.q: How many extra days did the teacher give Zubin?
qa.a: The teacher gave him three extra days.

qa.q: What does Zubin looking at the floor suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed once he was caught, even though he claimed he didn't think it was a big deal.

qa.q: What was fair about the teacher's response?
qa.a: She spoke to each student privately, explained why copying mattered, and gave Zubin a chance to redo the work and repair things with Ishita.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when she learned her notebook was copied?
qa.a: She probably felt used and upset, since she only meant to help, and worried she might be blamed too.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teen caught copying, understanding why originality matters and redoing the work.

passage:
Tuesday night, 11:40.
The English essay on 'A Place I Belong' is due tomorrow and I had NOTHING at nine. Dilnaz texted, 'Just use the chatbot, everyone does, then change a few words.' She even sent me hers to 'get ideas'. I opened it. It was good. Really good. Too smooth, honestly, it didn't sound like her at all.
I sat there for ages with my finger on the copy button. Then I thought: Ma'am asked where I belong. A machine doesn't know I belong on Nani's roof in Lucknow, flying kites with my cousins. Nobody else can write that.
So I wrote it myself. It's messy. Two paragraphs are too long. But every word is mine, and I actually cried a bit writing the kite part.
Going to sleep. — Zeenat

qa.q: What was the title of Zeenat's English essay?
qa.a: 'A Place I Belong'.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling while hovering over the copy button?
qa.a: Zeenat was tempted by the easy shortcut but uneasy, because the essay didn't sound like a real person.

qa.q: Why did writing it without help matter for this particular essay?
qa.a: It asked about Zeenat's own life, so only Zeenat could describe Nani's roof and the kites honestly.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see Zeenat's choice if she hears about it?
qa.a: She might feel a little defensive about using the chatbot, or start wondering what her own essay missed.

grounding: A teen resists copying and an AI-written shortcut and sees why their own original work matters.

passage: The phone-repair shop near the Nandgaon bus stand had one computer, and the owner's nephew, Bhola, swore it could write anything. "Type 'essay on groundwater, Class 10', Ramesh, and in one minute it's done. Neat English. Madam will never know." Ramesh watched the cursor blink. His own draft sat folded in his pocket: two pages in pencil, full of crossings-out, about the dry well behind his grandfather's field. Vidya, buying a recharge at the counter, glanced over. "Madam asked what we saw in our own village," she said. "Will the machine know your well?" Ramesh thought of the rope marks on the stone, of Dada measuring how far the bucket dropped each summer. The machine would give him perfect sentences about somebody else's water. "Leave it," he told Bhola. That night he copied his pencil draft out neatly and added Dada's summer measurements at the end.

qa.q: What was Ramesh's own draft about?
qa.a: The dry well behind his grandfather's field.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he watched the cursor blink?
qa.a: Ramesh felt tempted but uneasy; the neat essay was one click away while his own messy draft sat in his pocket, and Vidya's question tipped him towards pride in his real work.

qa.q: What small step would help Ramesh the next time a shortcut is offered?
qa.a: Ramesh could ask what the teacher actually wants to see, as Vidya did, and remember that details like Dada's measurements are what make the work his own.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Ramesh's choice?
qa.a: Vidya would likely respect it; her question was only a nudge, and he chose his own observations over neat borrowed sentences.

grounding: A small-town teenager turns down a machine-written essay and hands in his own observations of the village well.

passage: Sunday night in Johannesburg, and Dalia's history essay was due at eight the next morning. Her cousin Thabo, a year ahead, slid a folder across the kitchen table. "Same question last year. I got a distinction. Change a few words and go to sleep." Dalia opened it. Clean paragraphs about the city's early gold mines, quotes she would never have found. Her chest loosened, then tightened. If she handed this in and got praised, the praise would belong to Thabo. And in June there would be an exam, no folder allowed. She closed it. "Can you just show me how you found the sources?" Thabo shrugged, a little stung, then pulled up a chair. They worked until eleven. Her essay came out plainer than his, with one argument she was sure was her own.

qa.q: When was Dalia's history essay due?
qa.a: At eight the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Dalia's chest loosen and then tighten when she opened the folder?
qa.a: Dalia felt relieved at first that the work was done, then uneasy, because any praise would belong to Thabo and the June exam would still find her unprepared.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Dalia, and why?
qa.a: Asking Thabo how he found the sources worked: she got real help with the method while the essay stayed her own.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Dalia closes the folder?
qa.a: Thabo feels a little stung that his offer is turned down, but pulling up a chair suggests he accepts her choice and is willing to help in a better way.

grounding: A teenager in South Africa refuses to copy her cousin's old essay and asks him to teach her how to research instead.

passage: Study hour in the hostel reading room, and Keerthana had written four lines of her poem and crossed out three. Across the table, Chaitanya turned his tablet towards her. "Asked the chat tool for a poem about the monsoon. Look. Rhymes and everything." It was smooth, full of words like "silver" and "eternal". Keerthana's own line said the rain sounded like her mother frying mustard seeds. Beside his, it looked silly. "Do it," he whispered. "Two minutes." She typed half the request, then stopped. Ms Fernandes had said she wanted to hear "your ear, not the internet's". Keerthana deleted the words, kept the mustard seeds, and wrote six more lines about the leaking corridor roof and the warden's squeaking slippers. When the bell rang, she had a rough poem that sounded only like her.

qa.q: What did Keerthana's own line compare the rain to?
qa.a: Her mother frying mustard seeds.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she compared her line with the tablet poem?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and tempted, because her line looked silly beside the smooth one, and she even started typing the request.

qa.q: How could Ms Fernandes support students like Keerthana when a shortcut is this easy?
qa.a: Ms Fernandes could keep praising specific personal details like the mustard seeds, so students see that their own observations are what earn credit.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Keerthana's poem compared with his own?
qa.a: Chaitanya may think hers is rougher, but if the class responds to her real details, he might notice his borrowed poem has nothing of him in it.

grounding: A hostel student nearly asks a chat tool for a poem, then keeps her own imperfect lines because the teacher wants her voice.

passage:
Dear Vidya Ma'am,
I need to tell you something about my history project.
Last night, at midnight, I was stuck. I pasted the question into an AI tool, and it wrote the whole essay in ten seconds. It was better than anything I could write. I nearly submitted it.
Then I read it again and realised I couldn't explain half of it. If you asked me one question, I'd be caught. Worse, I wouldn't have learnt anything.
So I deleted it and wrote my own. It's shorter and messier, and I'm submitting it one day late.
I'm sorry about the delay. I'd rather be late than dishonest.
Tanvir

qa.a: Ten seconds.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when realising half the essay couldn't be explained?
qa.a: Tanvir felt uneasy and ashamed, knowing it wasn't really Tanvir's work.

qa.q: What choice did Tanvir make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Tanvir deleted the AI essay and wrote an original one, choosing learning and honesty over a perfect but fake submission.

qa.q: How might Vidya Ma'am feel reading this email?
qa.a: Vidya Ma'am would likely respect the honesty and may be more understanding about the late submission.

grounding: A teen writes to a teacher about resisting submitting an AI-written essay.

passage:
You asked about the moment I learnt why originality matters. So, I'm Kiran, and in Class 10, my friend Ramesh offered me his old science project. "Same topic. Just change the name. Nobody will know."
I was drowning that week. Three tests, a cousin's wedding. I said yes. I had the file open. I was typing my name.
Then I looked at the conclusion. Ramesh had written, "This experiment taught me patience." And I thought, it didn't teach me anything. I didn't do it.
I closed the file. I told my teacher I needed two more days. She gave them. I did a simpler experiment on plant growth, and it was ugly and half the seeds died.
But when she asked me about it, I could answer everything. And I remember it even now.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's conclusion say?
qa.a: "This experiment taught me patience."

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when Kiran said yes to Ramesh's offer?
qa.a: Kiran felt overwhelmed and desperate with three tests and a wedding that week.

qa.q: What choice inside the story did Kiran make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Kiran asked the teacher for two more days and did a simpler experiment, which meant real learning and no dishonesty.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Kiran turning down his project?
qa.a: Ramesh might be surprised, since he offered it to help, but may come to see why Kiran wanted original work.

grounding: A young person tells an interviewer how Kiran chose original work over copying a friend's project.

passage:
I'm Baljeet. The night before the maths assignment was due, someone shared a document in our class group with all the answers.
Most people copied. I did too, honestly. Charu, who sits next to me, didn't.
Next day I saw her notebook. She'd done half the questions, with crossings out, and written "Stuck here — will ask" next to question six.
The teacher noticed that twenty people had the same wrong answer on question nine. She gave all of us zero for that assignment. Charu got marks for the half she'd done, and the teacher spent lunch helping her with question six.
I don't know if Charu felt tempted. She didn't say. But she didn't look worried.

qa.q: How many people had the same wrong answer on question nine?
qa.a: Twenty people.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when the teacher gave everyone else zero?
qa.a: Charu likely felt calm and relieved that her honest, incomplete work was valued.

qa.q: What did Charu do that others could copy?
qa.a: Charu did what she could honestly and marked where she was stuck, so she could get help instead of hiding gaps.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see Charu's choice?
qa.a: Baljeet admits copying and notices Charu stayed honest and calm, without knowing if she was tempted.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen resist a shared answer document and do honest work.

passage:
Monday. The history project was due Thursday. Vinita sent Imran her finished file at 9 p.m. "Just change the words a bit. Everyone does it."
Imran stared at it. It was good. His own was two paragraphs and a heading.
Tuesday. He didn't open her file again, though he kept thinking about it. He went to the library at lunch and found two books on the salt march. He wrote badly, crossed out, wrote again. At night he messaged Vinita, "Thanks, but I'll do mine."
"Your loss," she wrote.
Thursday. His project was shorter and messier than hers. But when Ma'am asked him a question about his sources, he could answer without looking. Walking out, he felt oddly light. Two other students' projects came back with "Please see me" on them.

qa.q: How did Imran feel walking out on Thursday?
qa.a: Imran felt oddly light and relieved, because the work was his own and he could answer Ma'am's questions.

qa.a: Because Imran actually learned the topic and could explain his sources; copied work would have looked better but left him unable to answer.

passage:
Harish, you're asking why I won't just let an app write your essay. Sit, I'll tell you a thing.
When I was sixteen, there was a district essay prize. The topic was my own town. I found an old magazine article that said everything better than I could. I copied three paragraphs, changed a few words, and won second prize.
At the prize function, the judge, an old schoolteacher, asked me to talk about the river bit, the part I'd copied. I couldn't. I stood there, my face burning. She didn't shame me in public. She just looked at me, and that was worse.
The next week I went to her house and told her the truth. She said, "Write it again, your own way." I did. It was worse. But it was mine. That's why your Zeenat Khala is so strict about this.

qa.q: What prize did young Zeenat win?
qa.a: She won second prize in a district essay competition.

qa.q: How did young Zeenat feel when asked about the river part?
qa.a: Young Zeenat felt ashamed and trapped, with a burning face, because she couldn't talk about words that weren't hers.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zeenat's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Going to the judge's house to tell the truth mattered, because it let her take responsibility and rewrite the essay honestly.

qa.q: How might the old schoolteacher have felt when young Zeenat came to confess?
qa.a: The teacher was probably disappointed at first, but moved and respectful that the girl came back on her own.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting a copied essay and why original work matters, as a lesson against AI shortcuts.

passage:
At 10:40 p.m., with the English essay due at midnight on the school portal, the power went out in Vidya's building. Her laptop had 20% battery. She had one paragraph.
Gopika texted: "Just use the AI thing. Two minutes. Nobody can tell."
Vidya almost did. Her finger was on the app. Then she thought about how the essay was supposed to be about her own grandmother's village, and how no app knew that.
Instead she wrote fast, by the light of her phone, a shorter essay in her own words. At 11:50 she submitted it, three paragraphs instead of five. Then she emailed Ms Fernandes: "The power went out. I've submitted what I wrote myself. Could I add the last two paragraphs tomorrow?"
Ms Fernandes replied in the morning: "Yes. Thank you for being honest."

qa.q: How many paragraphs did Vidya submit at 11:50?
qa.a: Three paragraphs instead of five.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling with her finger on the app?
qa.a: Vidya felt tempted and stressed by the deadline, but uneasy that no app knew her grandmother's village.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Submitting a shorter essay of her own and honestly asking for more time worked, because the teacher trusted her and she kept her work original.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Vidya's choice on hearing about the extension?
qa.a: Gopika might be surprised that honesty worked out, and maybe feel a little uncomfortable about suggesting the shortcut.

grounding: Shows a teen under time pressure choosing original writing over an AI-written submission and asking for an extension honestly.

passage: At 11:40 on a Sunday night, Gautam's history essay on the salt march had exactly one paragraph. His classmate Kishore had messaged an hour earlier: "Just paste the question into the chatbot, bro. Takes two minutes. Ma'am never checks." Gautam opened the chatbot tab, typed half the prompt, and stopped. Last month Mrs. Rao had read out his essay on the Partition trains, the one with his Dadi's story in it, and the whole class had gone quiet. Nobody else could have written that one. He deleted the prompt. He pulled out his notes, messy blue ink and arrows everywhere, and wrote until 1:15. The middle section came out clumsy. On Monday Kishore grinned and said, "Full marks, easy." Gautam shrugged, tired but strangely light, and handed in his own four pages.

qa.q: What time did Gautam finish writing his essay?
qa.a: He wrote until 1:15 on Sunday night.

qa.q: Why did Gautam stop halfway through typing the prompt?
qa.a: He remembered feeling proud when the class went quiet over his Partition essay with his Dadi's story, and he felt uneasy about handing in words that were not his.

qa.q: What small step helped Gautam get started on his own?
qa.a: He pulled out his handwritten notes instead of staring at a blank page, so the essay could grow from material he already had.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Gautam's choice?
qa.a: Kishore probably thinks Gautam wasted a night on something a chatbot could do in two minutes, and may not understand why owning the work mattered to him.

grounding: Shows a teen turning down an AI-written shortcut and choosing to hand in work that is truly his own.
